[ir] Support packages with keywords as names (contextual keywords)

Fix DoesErase propagation logic in resource sharing pass. Previously, DoesErase assumed that if the value of a @node is known to be 0 that it would stop the propagation of some @source whose def-use chain included @node. Now, we check known operations like "And" and "Or" to see if an operand not in the def-use chain of @source causes the operation to not be influenced by whatever value @source has.

Consider this example operation "and(0b101010..., 0b010101...)". Under the old approach, we would incorrectly claim the operation erases its source (LHS or RHS, regardless). However, it is obvious that these values are chosen very carefully to result in the operation being == 0.

Clarify logic around choosing the quickcheck evaluator.

Previously, the quickcheck evaluator piggy-backed on the comparison runner which meant if you ran the interpreter with --evaluator=jit --comparison=none you'd get a confusing message about not running the quickcheck tests because the jit is disabled. Avoid using a JitRuntime over multiple Package*s in jit_channel_queue_test

This test was (correctly) transforming xls::Value into the jit representation used by our llvm jit. The JitRuntime which holds a map<xls::Type*, llvm::Type*> as a type cache was not invalidated or cleared for each Package*. This meant that if 2 tests happened to allocate xls::Type*s with the same pointer and they are different sizes then the tests could fail due to different pieces of code not agreeing on how much data needed to be copied. This caused the tests to read uninitialized memory.

To fix this rewrite the jit_channel_queue_test such that each run initializes its own JitRuntime* avoiding any sharing of caches.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 825166312

Disallow ram configurations with latency != 1 for now.

Ram latency needs to be rethought to support values != 1 (see google/xls#1053).  It is currently broken. The current behavior is to add a scheduling constraint of $LATENCY between request and response. This is not an unreasonable thing to do, but to get the correct behavior the receive on the response channel should wait $LATENCY cycles before capturing the response. It currently waits 1. Also, the response channel should have a $LATENCY-deep FIFO to catch responses in case of stalling (or a credit-like mechanism to stall the request side). Instead, the current behavior is a depth-1 FIFO that can overflow, resulting in lost data and potential deadlock. Until these issues are confronted, it seems best to require latency to be 1 as that is the only correctly supported configuration.

When a (logical) shift amount is an interval with lower bound > 0, some bits are guaranteed to be zero. For left shifts, the lower bound indicates the number of trailing zeros. For right shifts, the lower bound indicates the number of leading zeros.

The previous implementation incorrectly applied the lower bound without checking direction, resulting in modeling trailing zeros for both left and right shifts.

Introduce DataFlowLazyNodeInfo base class.

This class is meant to make it easy to implement lazy analyses that track leaf nodes, bits in this case as only Functions are supported, through compound operations (eg tuples) and invokes to their sources.

Note that if an operation is not explicitly supported, then the analysis will merge all of its operands. For example, for an array slice, the start index will be merged with the array being sliced. This can produce false positives, that is trace a node back to more sources than strictly necessary.

This was implemented in order to enable XLS[cc] to track direct-in values through function slices, from input parameters to continuation outputs. This allows direct-ins not to be placed into StateElements.

Also remove currently unneeded optional return to LazyNodeData::GetInfo().

[ir] Introduce `ScheduledBlock` for representing scheduled pipelines

We introduce `ScheduledBlock` as a new IR construct, inheriting from `xls::Block`, to represent logic with an explicit pipeline control flow. `ScheduledBlock`s contain explicit pipeline stage boundaries, where each stage is bracketed by control signals indicating input and output validity.

This enables representing pipeline implementations directly within XLS IR, via:

*   A `ScheduledBlockBuilder` for programmatic construction.
*   A new `scheduled_block` construct in textual `.ir` files, containing `controlled_stage` blocks for each pipeline stage. We support both parsing from & writing to this format.

We intend to use this to support incremental lowering in XLS Codegen 1.5 - so we also introduce a `VerifyOptions` struct to the verifier functions, replacing the `codegen` boolean parameter. A new option, `incomplete_lowering`, is added to allow for verification of partially lowered block IR.

Fix new FSM bug in RemovePassThroughs()

When feedback passthroughs are removed, this can change the order of ContinuationValues seen by an input phi, that is which value the phi sees in each activation, corrupting the logic of the block.

This change disallows removing feedback passthroughs in RemovePassThroughs().

This creates a QoR problem that sometimes direct-ins get stored in StateElements. This happens because feedbacks are always stored in StateElements, even if they are sourced from direct-ins. This is because, for example "value+1" is still marked direct-in as long as value is marked direct-in.

To address this, the pass RemovePassthroughFeedbacks() is added that removes feedback passthroughs only if they all feed in the same value to the phi as the feed-forward input.

Note that more comprehensive and/or elegant solutions could include:
- Doing virtual unrolling before continuation optimization
- Removing feedback passthroughs if they pass a more sophisticated analysis that they don't cross other feedbacks on the same phi.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 852954022

[codegen 1.5] Fix one-shot-send logic

We accidentally tied the `reset_one_shot` logic to the already-done register's reset as well as its data & logic-enable lines, rather than connecting it to the block's reset port. If interpreted as active-low, this caused us to reset at the completely wrong times; if interpreted as active-high, it would instead block normal resetting.

This lets us re-enable the last RandomStalling test for the codegen 1.5 block-conversion pipeline. While we were working, we refactored the test logic for clearer & less verbose error reporting. The test parameterization was also updated to use a different parameter space, cutting out redundant test scenarios.

[codegen 1.5] Add reset requirement for valid-output control

If lowering a function with a valid-output control signal, we should always have a reset signal; otherwise we can end up with (pipeline_depth - 1) cycles of garbage at the valid-output signal, potentially signaling "valid" when the output is very much not valid. This required adding reset signal support to our unit tests' RunFunctionalTest logic for this pass.

While we're at it, we also ensure that the source return value is always available in the last pipeline stage by inserting an identity node if necessary - which can be necessary when lowering a no-op function that directly returns one of its inputs. (This mostly only comes up in testing.)

Adds support for DSLX bit vectors wider than 64 bits in the C++ transpiler.

Previously, bit vectors larger than 64 bits were incorrectly represented as `(u)int64_t`. This change introduces a new representation for wide bit vectors: `std::bitset<N>`.

A new class hierarchy is introduced:
-   `BitVectorCppEmitter`: Base class for bit vector emitters.
-   `CppIntBitVectorEmitter`: Handles bit vectors up to 64 bits, using standard C++ integer types.
-   `RawBitVectorCppEmitter`: Handles bit vectors larger than 64 bits, using `std::bitset<N>`.

Enums are a special case; their underlying type is capped at 64 bits in the C++ representation, even if the DSLX type is wider.

Helper functions `FillBitSet` and `FromBitSet` are added to `xls::Bits` to facilitate conversion between `Bits` and `std::bitset<N>`.

Fix bug where TI is willing to infer parametrics from auto literals.

In a case like `assert_eq(0, some_stuff)` we should not be using the `0` to infer the parametric argument for `assert_eq`. some_stuff, being a named entity, must have a type derived from some explicit info, and therefore we should be solving for the parametric using that, and applying the result to the `0`.

Before this change, we would ultimately infer conflicting types for the two arguments in this example, and it would fail to compile. We would try parametric solution using the arguments from left to right, and we would cache their individual types yielded by ConvertSubtree as we went.

The sensible rule here seems to be to just never infer parametrics from auto types, for the same reason you can't declare a var using auto types; the result could be surprising. Therefore the example `some_parametric_fn(0)`, where there is not a different argument to serve as a better candidate, would now just be rejected.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 868278235

Avoid creating def-use constraints for nodes which are dead after synthesis.

Dead-after-synthesis nodes (ie nodes which are ultimately only visible from trace, cover or assert nodes) are modeled as having zero delay since synthesis tools will be able to recognize their computation plays no part in the ultimate chip design and so can be ignored. Unfortunately we were still scheduling these nodes as normal (albeit with zero delay). This works but can cause scaling issues due to the addition of (trivial) constraints. By instead excluding these from the constraint model and instead doing the trivial scheduling as a final fixup step the schedulers performance can be drastically improved.

We have seen as codegen times fall by more than half on some designs.

fix: resource sharing pass legalize foldings to avoid cycle

The following tricky situation was missed by `LegalizeSequenceOfFolding` for the longest time now:

Consider if B <- A <- X and D <- C <- Y are two def-use chains; folding X into D to produce D' makes a new def-use chain B <- A <- D' <- C <- Y. Folding Y into B would cause a cycle because B now depends on Y via D'.

To mitigate this, we now use NodeBackwardDependencyAnalysis along with a map<Node*, set<Node*>> that tracks what nodes are merged together by accepted folds in order to determine if the next fold would be between two nodes that would be in a def-use chain due to previous accepted folds.

[opt] Aggressively optimize our BDD usage for improved performance

1. We optimize BDD implication checks by introducing a new variant of IfThenElse which only looks for constant outcomes, and terminates early if the result cannot be constant. This dates back to the paper that our BDD implementation is based on (Brace, Rudell, & Bryant, 1990).

2. We replace our explicit use of a `std::variant` to manage freelist entries with a sentinel "variable" value in our BddNode structure; this should make our node storage a bit more memory efficient, mostly by avoiding padding.

3. When the ITE cache gets too large, we now switch over to a lossy cache with fast lookups (no probing) and bounded size. Experiments show this avoids cache-miss overhead that could previously really hurt our performance on large designs. We currently hardcode this to cut over at 1M entries; we may tune it more later.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 888833830

Remove filters from BDD computation

For a long time we've had filters to make bdd computation proactively abort calculation if it sees particular operations or operations with arguments/results of particular sizes. This was done to save time and memory space. Recent tests however have shown that these filters do not actually save very much time and the BDD Gc is capable of ameliorating the memory cost of this computation.

Therefore we are simplifying things to basically only filter out multiplication/division/mod operations and rely only on bdd saturation for all other computation. This has a slight impact on opt time (5-10% depending on target) but can significantly improve our quality of result on some designs.

Refine GetDeadAfterSynthesisNodes to give more accurate results.

For procs we would give a rather conservative analysis where we would consider `Next` and `StateRead` nodes always alive even if the `Next` feeds a `StateRead` which is only read by 'dead-after-synthesis' nodes. This extends the analysis to recognize these situations.

The SDC scheduler is updated to use ASAP scheduler to actually place dead-after-synthesis nodes. This ensures that any state elements present in this set will respect the II constraints (since that is observable in simulation). This ASAP schedule cannot fail because we can always worst case put everything in exactly one stage at the very end as a valid assignment because by definition since the states are dead after synthesis they cannot be blocked behind any outputs and so the stage is unobservable.

Fix for redundant break statements in nested scopes.

Generated by Gemini. Its explanation:

✦ The PipelinedLoopOuterExit test case fails when the break on line 10929 of the test file is present because of a bug in xls/contrib/xlscc/translator.cc where
  relative_break_condition was being overwritten by subsequent break statements instead of being accumulated.

  Root Cause Analysis
  In translator.cc, within the GenerateIR_Stmt function, the handling for clang::BreakStmt and clang::ContinueStmt used simple assignment (=) for relative_break_condition and
  relative_continue_condition.

   1 // Original buggy code in translator.cc
   2 context().relative_break_condition = context().relative_condition_bval(loc);

  When a loop body contains multiple break statements, such as:

   1 if (x > 10) {
   2   if (x == 55) {
   3     exit_function = true;
   4     break; // Break 1
   5   }
   6   break;  // Break 2
   7 }
  The translator processes both break statements. When x == 55, Break 1 correctly sets the relative_break_condition. However, the translator continues to process Break 2. Although Break 2 is
  logically unreachable in C++ when Break 1 is taken, the translator still evaluates it with its current relative_condition. Because Break 1 calls and_condition(0) to make the rest of the
  block a no-op, the relative_condition for Break 2 becomes 0. The assignment relative_break_condition = 0 then overwrites the valid break condition from Break 1, causing the generated IR to
  lose the signal to exit the loop.

  Fix
  The fix involves using or_condition_util to OR the new break/continue condition with any existing ones, ensuring that all possible exit paths are preserved.

   1 // Fixed code in translator.cc
   2 context().or_condition_util(context().relative_condition_bval(loc),
   3                             context().relative_break_condition, loc);

  This ensures that if any break in the current context is triggered, the relative_break_condition remains true. I have applied this fix to both BreakStmt (for both for and switch bodies)
  and ContinueStmt in translator.cc.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 897843053

Simplify UDiv/SDiv by variable power of two.

Adds a pattern to replace `x / (2^L << k)`:

- For unsigned division (`UDiv`), this is all ones if the divisor is overshifted (and thus zero), and otherwise `(x >> L) >> k`.
- For signed division (`SDiv`), this has one more case. The cases handled are:
    - `k + L >= bit_width`: Division by zero, resulting in `(x < 0) ? min_neg : max_pos`.
    - `k + L == bit_width - 1`: Division by `min_neg`, resulting in `(x == min_neg) ? 0 : 1`.
    - Otherwise, we can compute `x / (2^L << k)` as `((x + bias) >> L) >> k`, where `bias` is `(2^L << k) - 1` if `x` is negative and `0` otherwise.

Also adds a pattern to simplify `X / (Y << K)` for any `Y`, which will take care of (e.g.) `X / (3 << K)`.

Add design document for division simplification in XLS.

This document outlines a design for simplifying division operations where the divisor takes a small set of values, using PartialInfoQueryEngine to analyze possible divisor values. The design covers cases where divisors are powers of two, general constants, or a hybrid mix, and suggests implementation in three phases. Divisions by powers of two can be simplified to either a shift-by-encode or to division by constants (which will later be reduced to shifts by constants), while divisions by general values can be simplified to division by constants (which will later be reduced to multiply-and-shift form).

[opt] Automatically skip known-no-op passes in pipelines

If a pass is invoked twice on the same IR, and made no changes the first time, then we know it should make no changes the second time. Rather than rerunning the pass and any associated analyses, we can skip this entirely.

To support this, we add the `GetRedundancyGuard` method to `PassBase`, so passes can declare their compatibility with this handling and publish a `config` string of all options affecting how the pass runs. Any pass that does not declare its compatibility with this system will run every time.

Certain passes are idempotent, meaning that if they're invoked twice in sequence, the second invocation will *always* be a no-op. We add the `IsIdempotent` method to let these passes opt into this stronger behavior.

Add DecomposeDataflowPass to flatten compound data types.

This pass transforms IR by replacing operations on arrays and tuples with equivalent operations on their individual leaf elements (bits or empty tuples). This is achieved by using a dataflow visitor that tracks the decomposition of compound types.

Key transformations include:
-   Replacing array/tuple operations like ArrayIndex, ArrayUpdate, ArraySlice, ArrayConcat, TupleIndex with equivalent logic using Selects and operations on leaf elements.

-   Handling Select, PrioritySelect, and OneHotSelect by reconstructing them on the decomposed leaf elements.

This pass is intended for development and testing purposes, allowing analysis and optimization on a flattened representation of the IR.

Fix UAF/Iterator Invalidation issue in optimization context.

The OptimizationContext contains (among other things) a map from FunctionBase* to the topo sort of that function. This topo sort is stored in a list that is made to delete itself if the function is changed using a ChangeListener.

If one of the functionBases with this topo sort list is deleted the OptimizationContext was not notified so both a dangling pointer to the function and a (now detached) change listener was kept around.

This could lead to use after free and iterator invalidation issues.

First there is the obvious risk that if a pointer is reissued by the allocator map index operations could incorrectly return data for the old function.

More likely however if a new FunctionBase is created the resize of the map will cause UAF when we try to add the copied listeners onto the deleted function (and again when we try to delete the moved-away listeners for that matter).

This needs to be solved by having the change-listener inform the OptimizationContext that it needs to be deleted and not calling UnregisterChangeListener in this case because the function it's attached to is currently iterating over the list of change-listeners so modifying it could invalidate iterators.

dslx: prevent specialized spans from overlapping real source

This keeps fabricated specialization spans separate from real DSLX source spans. Specialized functions now live in their own synthetic source file identity, so invocation replacement no longer confuses unrelated real calls with nodes inside a synthesized function.

# Problem Solved

`InsertFunctionSpecialization()` was fabricating spans with synthetic line numbers but, for file-backed modules, reusing the real module filename. That allowed a specialized function's span to overlap unrelated source text in the same file.

During `ReplaceInvocationsInModule()`, that overlap could make `ContainedWithinFunction()` see:

- the AST parent chain says an invocation is outside the candidate caller
- the source span says it is inside

The mismatch trips the containment check and aborts the rewrite.

Minimized example:

```dslx
fn helper(x: u32) -> u32 { x }
fn unrelated(x: u32) -> u32 { helper(x) }
fn id<N: u32>(x: bits[N]) -> bits[N] { x }
```

After specializing `id`, the real `helper(x)` call in `unrelated` must never look like it belongs to the synthesized specialized function.

# What Changed

- `xls/dslx/frontend/function_specializer.cc`
  - Always assigns specialized functions a dedicated `<specialization:...>` pseudo-file instead of reusing the real DSLX source filename.
- `xls/dslx/type_system_v2/inference_table_utils.cc`
  - Accepts those specialization pseudo-files when rebuilding typechecked numeric values, so specialized modules still re-typecheck correctly.
- `xls/dslx/frontend/function_specializer_test.cc`
  - Updates the span expectation to require source-file separation.
  - Adds a regression test for the former containment-abort shape.

# Validation

- `bazel test //xls/dslx/frontend:function_specializer_test --test_output=errors`

Refactor XLS schedulers to use a common interface and allow for selecting scheduler for minimization workloads.

This change introduces a `Scheduler` abstract base class, and refactors `ASAP`, `MinCut`, and `SDC` scheduling algorithms to implement this interface. A new `RandomScheduler` is also added. The `run_pipeline_schedule` utility is updated to use this new interface. Additionally, a new option and flag `--find_bounds_strategy` are added, allowing a different scheduler (defaulting to the selected scheduling algorithm usually SDC) to be used for finding minimum clock period and worst-case throughput bounds, which can be faster than using the main scheduling strategy. Error handling in `run_pipeline_schedule` is also improved.

The 'random' scheduler is also updated to make use of the ASAP scheduler bounds to do a much better job at consistently choosing allowable schedules.

The previous run_pipeline_scheduleing had a number of subtle bugs around how its configuration was interpreted that have all been fixed up, requiring some changes to tests which relied on the previous behavior.

Testing is improved to check schedulers other than SDC. Many tests needed to be tweaked to account for the different ways these schedulers work.

This change introduces a new class, `VisibilityAnnotator`, which is an `IrAnnotator` that can be used to dump the IR with annotations showing the visibility BDD for each node. The `VisibilityAnalysis` class now provides an `annotator()` method to create an instance of this annotator. A test case is updated to demonstrate the use of the annotator by recording the annotated IR.

This creates output like:

```
fn MutuallyExclusivePrioritySelectCases(op: bits[1] id=1 visible[1], x: bits[4] id=2 visible[1], y: bits[4] id=3 visible[1]) -> bits[4] {
  add.4: bits[4] = add(x, y, id=4) visible[x0]
  sub.5: bits[4] = sub(x, y, id=5) visible[!x0]
  ret priority_sel.6: bits[4] = priority_sel(op, cases=[add.4], default=sub.5, id=6) visible[1]
}
```

Fix reassociation pass fuzzing failure with wrapped values in unsigned mode.

Disable narrowing (width reduction) in the reassociation pass for unsigned
expressions that contain negated terms (subtractions).

Previously, the pass would narrow intermediate operations to save bits.
However, if an intermediate subtraction wrapped (e.g., p1 - X where p1 < X),
it resulted in a two's complement representation of a negative number in the
narrower width (e.g., 2^593 - L). When this wrapped value was subsequently
zero-extended to a wider width, the wrap-around carry was preserved as a
positive value, preventing correct cancellation with other terms later in the
tree.

By disabling narrowing when negated terms are present in unsigned mode, we
force all intermediate operations to be computed at the final target width,
ensuring that wrapping behavior is consistent and cancels out correctly.

[solvers] Simplify & optimize our Z3 translations

Swaps out the eager bit-blasting implementations based on the abstract evaluator, replacing them with more efficient translations where possible. We also improve the implementation for PrioritySelect.

Examples:

- Decode: Use a symbolic shift left (1 << x), since Z3 already matches our semantics.
- OneHot: Use a native implementation; use the (x & -x) trick to isolate the least-significant 1 for LSB priority, and convert MSB priority into LSB in order to take advantage of the same trick.
- Encode: Use direct mask creation for each bit, followed by concatenation.

For PrioritySelect, we use a recursive balanced binary ITE tree, which shows a pretty substantial speedup on 64 cases (~38%).

Also adds a few benchmarks to measure the impact of these changes.

Fix Bazel cache cleanup in nightly OSS CI.

The nightly Ubuntu CI workflow was failing during the "Clean Bazel Cache"
step, which prevented the subsequent "Save Bazel Cache" step from running.
This locked the CI into a loop where it always built from scratch, leading
to extremely long build times and "RPC deadline exceeded" errors.

The failure was caused by Bzlmod/Bazel 8 directory layout changes. Bzlmod uses canonical repository names (e.g., prefixing PDKs with the extension/module name), which broke the exact path matches in the cleanup script.

This CL fixes the issue by:
- Preventing failed commands from interrupting the nightly before cache save.
- Adding wildcards (e.g., `*org_theopenroadproject_asap7*` to the globs to robustly match Bzlmod's canonical repository names.

Also add `*com_google_skywater_pdk*` PDKs to the cleanup, which seems to actually be larger than asap7.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 938297959

Fix cache corruption by deleting Bazel .marker files in nightly CI.

The previous cache cleanup implementation (cl/938231095) maintained a trailing slash in the cleanup globs (e.g., `external/*com_google_skywater_pdk*/`). Because of the trailing slash, the glob only matched and deleted the repository directories, leaving behind the corresponding marker files (https://bazel.build/contribute/codebase#fetch-repos).

This was previously a silent issue under the WORKSPACE system, but with the recent migration to Bzlmod (Bazel 8), Bazel seems to be much stricter about repository caching. Bzlmod trusts the remaining marker files and assumes the repositories are already fetched, skipping the download. This resulted in subsequent runs (like PR builds) failing during analysis due to empty directories ("BUILD file not found").

This CL fixes the issue by removing the trailing slashes from the cleanup globs for ASAP7, SkyWater, and JDK, ensuring both the directories and their `.marker` metadata files are deleted to force a clean re-download.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 939969899

An immutable sorted vector

We often need to deterministically iterate over some `const` collection. In some cases, we could use a `std::vector` and sort it, and do so at the time of creating the collection. In API signatures, `std::vector` doesn't capture this bit of information - i.e. that the producer took steps to guarantee determinism (see next para); or that the consumer intends to iterate deterministically. `SortedVector` does.

`SortedVector` is not formally guaranteeing this property; it relies on the user defining a meaningful strong ordering. It's easy, though, to make sure the production of these things is done correctly (i.e. it's easy to spot a SortedVector returned with naked pointers, sorted naturally rather than a custom comparer, for example)

The design is slightly more complicated than aliasing std::vector, to also block vector mutation APIs. Contents could still be mutated, but traversal order wouldn't change.

If none are provided, then the function would return always_visible. If every edge in the def-use DAG from `node` down to terminal nodes is provided, then the expression would be exact, assuming no BDD overflow, and conservative otherwise. Providing only a subset of the entire DAG would produce a smaller and conservative expression, perhaps less conservative if that subset is chosen wisely.

BuildVisibilityIRExpr had a bug where the short-circuit path when you provided a single-element conditional_edges set assumed that that single edge was a sufficient visibility expression to account for every path through the DAG. This assumption was made because resource sharing was using BuildVisibilityIRExpr in this way if it could prove mutual exclusivity via SingleSelectVisibilityAnalysis.

For more context:

* BuildVisibilityIRExprFromEdges computes visibility as OR(vis_node_through_user_i AND vis_user_i) where if the edge (node->user) is NOT in conditional_edges we assume vis_node_through_user_i is always true. This function is conservative. Using conditional_edgescan help prevent BDD overflow.
* The test helper BuildDefaultVisibilityExpr uses GetEdgesForMutuallyExclusiveVisibilityExpr to determine a subset of conditional_edges that helps BuildVisibilityIRExprFromEdgesnot overflow.

Add untimed proc unrolling and output equivalence testing.

This change introduces `UnrollProcToUntimedFunction` in `proc_testutils`, which converts a Proc into a Function for a fixed number of activations, modeling channels as FIFOs with a given depth. This allows for testing proc equivalence in an untimed manner, focusing on the sequence of values sent and received.

The existing `UnrollProcToFunction` has been refactored to use a more general visitor structure with concepts for input generation and output consumption. Helper functions `CreateFifoPush` and `CreateFifoPop` are added to model FIFO behavior.

A new test utility, `ScopedVerifyProcOutputEquivalence`, is added to `ir_equivalence_testutils` to verify that the output behavior of a Proc remains unchanged after modifications, using the new untimed unrolling.

To support these changes, `BValue` now has equality and hashing support, and `FunctionBase` gains a `ReorderParams` method, used by `FunctionBuilder::SetParamOrder` to ensure consistent parameter ordering in the generated functions.

This tool is made to allow for testing of passes which adjust the activation boundaries of procs.

Fix channel queue UB when read/writing zero bytes.

Make sure we don't memcpy() zero bytes to/from nullptrs.

The test `//xls/jit:jit_channel_queue_test` was failing

 * ThreadSafeJitChannelQueueTest/ChannelQueueTestBase.ChannelWithEmptyTuple/0
 * LockLessJitChannelQueueTest/ChannelQueueTestBase.ChannelWithEmptyTuple/0

with current clang.

These were testing with `Value::Tuple({})`, which results in a
`channel_element_size_` of zero. With zero size, the optimization in the
`std::vector<uint8_t> buffer(queue.element_size())` realizes it
doesn't need any memory and optimizes to be a `nullptr` data...

Then `memcpy()` attempt to copy zero bytes to a nullptr is UB, and at
that point everything else was optimized away, so queue->GetSize() returned
wrong values.

(test failure: https://github.com/google/xls/actions/runs/29505219434/job/87644096322?pr=4568#step:8:1643 )

Split ProcStateOptimizationPass into ProcStateEliminationPass and ProcStateFSMPass.

Initially proc_state_opt was our only optimization pass which touched proc state elements. Initially it did simple DCE style optimizations to eliminate unobservable or trivial state elements. When the first real proc optimization was added (FSM optimization) we just placed it in this pass. As time went on many more passes which change proc state. Having a single pass which both does dead-code style trivial rewrites and a more complicated FSM rewrite named something as generic as 'ProcStateOptimizationPass' has become a problem.

This change splits the monolithic ProcStateOptimizationPass into two separate, more focused passes:
- ProcStateEliminationPass, which removes zero-width, constant, and unobservable state elements.
- ProcStateFSMPass, which optimizes implicit state machines by converting constant chains to binary-encoded state machines.

The optimization pipeline is updated to run these passes individually, running the elimination pass before and after the FSM pass to clean up redundant state. Tests and build targets are updated accordingly.

For now the pass pipeline is updated to simply do these optimizations right next to one another to avoid changing the results of optimization too much. With this greater level of granularity we likely want to be more thoughtful about how we distribute the proc state optimizations.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 961806049

Fix Verilog codegen for narrow array update indices

When codegen for Op::kArrayUpdate, target indexes were compared directly
against the 32-bit loop counter (index_expr == induction_var).

When index_expr was narrower than 32 bits, Verilog's context-determined
width rules expanded index_expr to 32 bits before applying the operation
creating the index. For example, if the index_expr is ~1. The 1 is expanded
to 32 bits first and then do ~ evaluated as 32'hFFFFFFFF (4294967295)
instead of 1'b1 zero-extended to 32'd1, causing the index comparison to
fail for all elements and reducing the array update to a no-op in generated
Verilog.

This change explicitly zero-extends narrow index expressions to 32 bits via
concatenation ({ (32 - width)'b0, index_expr }), creating a self-determined
context so unary operations evaluate at their native width before
comparison.

Fix `BuiltinNameDef` redirection, and parentage in `AstCloner`.

When cloning name references to builtins (like `token()` and `send`),
`AstCloner` previously kept the pointer to the **source** module's
`BuiltinNameDef`. If the source module was later deleted, this led to

dslx: reject duplicate match alternatives (#30)

* dslx: reject duplicate match alternatives with both source locations

## Summary

- Reject duplicate match patterns even when an occurrence is embedded in a `|`-separated alternative.
- Highlight both the original and duplicate source locations in the compiler error.
- Preserve valid grouped alternatives and existing duplicate-arm checks.
- Preserve a disabled regression for the separate pre-existing case where an enum type alias gives the same variant two spellings.

## Problem Solved

DSLX compared complete match arms when checking for duplicates. Consequently, an enum variant could appear in separate arms and the match would still compile:

```dslx
match value {
  E::A => u32:0,
  E::B | E::A => u32:1,
  E::C => u32:2,
}
```

The second `E::A` can never match, hiding unreachable code and copy-and-paste mistakes. This change rejects the program with a `TypeInferenceError` and reports both occurrences.

## Implementation

Track individual top-level match alternatives alongside the existing whole-arm duplicate check. Retain the first occurrence so the error can name its location and attach both source spans to the diagnostic.

Programs that previously compiled with duplicate exact match alternatives now intentionally fail compilation. Valid grouped alternatives and existing range or tuple overlap behavior remain unchanged.

Enum type aliases such as `type Alias = E;` can still spell the same member as `E::A` and `Alias::A`. That pre-existing semantic-equivalence case is intentionally not fixed here; a repository-conventional `DISABLED_` regression records the failing behavior for future work.

## Testing

- `bazel test //xls/dslx/type_system_v2:typecheck_module_v2_control_flow_test //xls/dslx/exhaustiveness:exhaustiveness_match_test //xls/dslx/type_system:typecheck_module_test`
- Regression coverage verifies both source spans, rejects the reported enum pattern, and accepts unique grouped alternatives.
- Direct compiler checks cover the checked-in diagnostic fixture, existing whole-arm duplicates, and non-exhaustive enum matches.
- Forcing `DISABLED_MatchEnumVariantDuplicatedThroughTypeAlias` to run with `--gtest_also_run_disabled_tests` fails as expected; normal execution passes 100 control-flow tests and reports one disabled test.

* dslx: explain unresolved duplicate enum-alias match cases

E::A and Alias::A denote the same enum member after type Alias = E,
but match validation compares source spellings and incorrectly accepts
an unreachable duplicate arm.

Record beside the disabled regression that fixing this requires
resolving enum-member identity before comparing match patterns.

[opt] Support lifting operations through OneHotSelect

This change introduces safety checks for lifting operations through OneHotSelect based on whether the operation preserves zero and distributes over bitwise OR. This allows more aggressive optimization of OneHotSelect nodes while maintaining correctness.

If the OneHotSelect's selector might be zero, lifting the operation is only safe if the operation preserves zero; i.e., replacing input X by 0 makes the output 0.

If the OneHotSelect's selector might have more than one bit set, lifting the operation is only safe if the operation distributes over bitwise OR; i.e., f(replace input X with A | B) produces the same result as replacing the result with f(replace input X with A) | f(replace input X with B).

`sed -i` is a GNU extension. BSD sed, as shipped on macOS, reads the next
argument as the backup suffix, so `sed -i "s,{x},$TESTDATA_DIR,g" FILE`
consumes the script as a suffix and then fails with

    sed: 1: "/private/var/tmp/_bazel ...": invalid command code v

The substitution never runs, leaving the literal `{x}` placeholders in the
generated runfiles manifest. package_bazel_build.py then reaches

    os.path.commonpath([path, self._bazel_execroot])

with a relative mapping and a resolved absolute execroot, and dies with
`ValueError: Can't mix absolute and relative paths`.

Rewrite through a temporary file, which behaves the same under both seds.

[solvers/symex] Add minimal symbolic execution engine

Implements a symbolic execution engine for XLS IR functions that systematically
discovers feasible execution paths through multiplexers and generates concrete
test vectors for each path.

Architecture:
Uses a clean, decoupled two-phase architecture:

1. Up-front IR Encoding (Z3EncodingVisitor):
   The entire function DAG is translated into Z3 ASTs in a single post-order
   pass up-front. By subclassing IrTranslator, all 50+ IR op translations
   (arithmetic, bitwise, tuples, bit-slices, comparisons) are reused directly.
   Multiplexers (Select, PrioritySelect) are intercepted and translated as
   unconstrained symbolic SSA variables rather than folded into monolithic
   nested ite(...) trees.

2. Incremental SMT Decision-Tree Traversal (SymExEngine):
   Path exploration operates as a depth-first search over multiplexer branch
   choices in topological order. At each branch, a solver frame is pushed
   (Z3_solver_push), the branch condition (C_k) and arm equality (V_mux == A_k)
   are asserted, and satisfiability is checked. Unsatisfiable branches are
   pruned immediately, backtracking early without exploring downstream nodes.

3. Leaf Test Generation:
   When a feasible leaf is reached, concrete satisfying parameter assignments
   are extracted from the solver model into a SymbolicPath.

Files:
- symex_engine.{h,cc}: Path exploration engine and solver orchestration.
- z3_encoding_visitor.{h,cc}: Subclass of IrTranslator providing free SSA mux
  variables and branch condition / arm equality encodings.
- z3_ir_translator.h: Moved context-borrowing constructor and NoteTranslation
  to protected, and added translations() const accessor to enable subclass
  extension.
- symbolic_path.{h,cc}: Data structures for paths, decisions, and tests.
- Tests:
  - symex_engine_test.cc: Path exploration, early pruning, and coverage.
  - z3_encoding_visitor_test.cc: Opcode, tuple, and mux translation.
  - symbolic_path_test.cc: Path condition and test vector accessors.
  - symex_e2e_test.cc: E2E ALU execution test with interpreter validation.

[solvers/symex] Skip multiplexers that cannot affect the result

Path exploration enumerated every arm of every multiplexer, so a functional
unit whose output is discarded on the current path still multiplied the path
count. In the ALU example that gives 3 opcodes x 2 overflow outcomes = 6 paths,
even though `overflow` only reaches the result on the ADD opcode.

This CL adds observability pruning. `Z3EncodingVisitor` encodes each
multiplexer as an opaque, unconstrained SSA variable, so a node's expression
mentions the variable of multiplexer `m` exactly when `m` is reachable from
that node without passing through another multiplexer. The new
`MuxObservability` uses that to answer, at each step of the traversal, whether
any arm choice at a given multiplexer can still reach the function's result.
One that cannot is an observability don't care: its selector is left
unconstrained, and the resulting path stands in for every combination of its
arms.

This requires deciding consumers before producers, so multiplexers are now
visited in reverse topological order. Observability is tracked per arm rather
than per multiplexer -- taking arm k marks the selector and arm k observable
and says nothing about the arms not taken -- so the same multiplexer can matter
under one arm choice of its consumer and be a don't care under another.

Pruning makes the path partition coarser but not wrong: paths remain mutually
exclusive, still cover the whole input domain, and still combine into an ITE
tree equivalent to the monolithic Z3 translation. The formal property harness
verifies all three. `SymExOptions::prune_unobservable` disables the
optimization.

`SymbolicPath::unobservable_muxes` records the skipped multiplexers, and
`symex_main` prints them as `Don't cares: ...` so it is visible why one path
covers several input combinations:

```
Path #2:
  Inputs:
    op = bits[2]:1
    a = bits[8]:255
    b = bits[8]:255
  Don't cares: add_out, add_status
  Result = (bits[1]:0, bits[8]:255)
```

Path counts on the existing examples:

| Benchmark           | Before | After |
| ------------------- | -----: | ----: |
| `execute_alu`       |      6 |     4 |
| `priority_encoder`  |     16 |     5 |
| `three_way_compare` |      3 |     3 |

Concolic inputs compose unchanged. They are asserted in the solver's base
frame, which stays active for every subsequent satisfiability check, so a
binding constrains every node regardless of when the traversal reaches it.

This change allows the number of solver threads used by QuickCheck proofs to be configured via:


ComparatorEquivalenceMapping signed <-> unsigned inequalities by swapping msb

The trick used is that when going between signed and unsigned inequalities, you can swap the msb bits to maintain equivalence.

Consider the conversion:

A  u[lt|le|gt|ge]  B    --->    A  s[lt|le|gt|ge]  B

When msb(A) == msb(B), unsigned <-> signed requires no input msb change. When msb(A) != msb(B), swapping the input's msb bit cancels out the fact that going from unsigned to signed flips the result.

For example, A ult B is always true if msb(A) == 0 and msb(B) == 1, while A slt B is always false under those msb conditions. This line of reasoning applies to the other directions and inequalities.

CompareToArithEquivalenceMapping: no widening by using MSB selection

Thanks to Eric Astor for pointing this out to me:

```
ult(a, b) = sel(msb(a) ^ msb(b), [msb(a - b), msb(b)])
slt(a, b) = sel(msb(a) ^ msb(b), [msb(a - b), msb(a)])
```

The rest of the CL ensures we have swapped operands and/or inverted the result to normalize our msb selection logic as though we're always operating on ult or slt.

One test assumes a binary `/bin/pwd` to exist, which might not

build: raise the macOS deployment minimum to 11.0

Set the host and target macOS minimums to 11.0. With a modern Apple SDK,
the 10.15 minimum makes the rules_cc_autoconf addchdir probe fail while
gnulib replaces the posix_spawn types. The resulting declarations
conflict with the SDK when building m4, a host tool used by GMP in the
Bitwuzla dependency chain.

Keeping the host minimum aligned is necessary even when a build already
overrides the target minimum to 11.0. This raises the supported minimum
for Intel macOS builds as well; Apple Silicon already requires macOS 11.

Reuse existing nodes in EquivalenceMapping::ApplyToOperands
